INTRODUCTION 
The reduction in size of waste material on waste redu cers is based on the same principle regardless of 
the size of the equipment. 
 
Waste material is fed into the hopper where it falls into, or accumulates on top of, the cutting chamber. As 
the cutter shafts rotate, the hooks on the cutters grab material, pull it downward, and force it between the 
fixed anvils, piercing, shredding, splitting or tear ing the material in the process, thus effecting size 
reduction. The processed material exits the bottom of  the cutting table and falls onto whatever discharge 
system is provided. 
 
Ample space exists between the anvils to permit aggregate, abrasives, small to medium sized stones and 
similar materials to fall through the cutting chamber  intact. This feature helps reduce accelerated wear to 
cutters and anvils that the processing of such materials would otherwise cause. 
 
The cutters are positioned on the cutter shaft such th at no two cutters are ever at the same point in thei r 
rotation. This arrangement focuses most of the avai lable shaft force on the one or two cutters passing 
between the anvils with the remaining force being av ailable to the cutters that follow and that may be in  
the process of grabbing material. 
 
• Cutting chamber size, shaft rotation speed, number of  cutters per shaft, and cutter style all combine 
to determine the amount of material the unit can process in a given time frame. 
 
• Cutting chamber size determines the volume of material that can be loaded into the cutting table. 
 
• Faster shaft rotation results in more material grab bing and processing. During normal processing 
each shaft rotates at a pre-set maximum speed. 
 
• Fewer cutters per shaft means larger gaps between th e anvils, decreasing the degree to which the 
waste material must be processed to pass through. 
 
• The final factor, cutter style, is limited to two opti ons. High Force Cutters are equipped with two hooks 
per side and have a modest sweep diameter. High Volume Cutters feature three hooks per side and a 
larger sweep diameter, and are capable of grabbing s ignificantly more material per pass. However, 
like increasing the number of cutters, this cutter style  has the affect of limiting the force that can be 
focused to break through and process more resistant materials. 
  
Resistant Material Processing 
A standard feature on all waste reducer models is th at each cutter shaft is driven by a dedicated closed-
loop hydrostatic drive. The hydraulic pressure, in each dedicated circuit, is proportional to the torque 
being utilized by its respective shaft. As resistance i ncreases, so do the required torque and, 
consequently, the hydraulic pressure. By constantly monitoring this pressure, it is possible to detect when 
a shaft has encountered sufficient resistance to require more torque than is normally available. 
 
When this condition occurs, the system automatically sacri fices shaft rotation speed to provide more 
torque and, therefore, more processing force. This is  similar to an automatic transmission, in an 
automobile, shifting into a lower gear long enough to climb a hill. As soon as the more resistant material is 
pushed or broken through, the required torque and the hydraulic pressure are reduced. 
 
If an object is encountered that is so resistant that  it refuses to be processed, even when the additiona l 
force is applied, the system reverses the rotation di rection of the effected shaft. This has the effect of 
rolling the resistant object across to the opposite s et of anvils. Since the waste reducer processes when 
the shafts rotate in either direction, the resistant  object is quickly re-grabbed and processing is again 
attempted. After a few seconds, the shaft rotation r eturns to its original direction. This sequence will be 
repeated until the material is successfully processed, or until sufficient time has passed, without 
resumption of normal operation, that the system deem s the object cannot be processed. Should this

Slow Speed Processing 
Normal speed processing of waste that has a significant low-density material content, such as film plastic 
or sheet paper may result in pieces becoming airborne and carried by momentum or the wind out of the 
hopper and into the surrounding area. This phenomen on is more likely to occur when no hopper 
extension is present and/or when High Volume Cutters are being utilized. 
 
To minimize this effect the operator may choose to temporarily run the waste reducer in slow-speed mode 
(if the controls permit slow speed). This option lim its the cutter shaft rotation speed, and reduces the 
tendency for the cutters to “toss” the lighter material. 
 
When operating in this manner, maximum shaft torque and processing force are available at all times. 
 
Waste Material Agitation 
All waste reducer control systems are supplied with multiple factory-set Auto Reverse Programs plus one 
user-configurable Auto Reverse Program. 
 
When any of these programs are active, the system forces the cutter shafts to reverse direction at pre-set 
intervals. On dual-shaft models, the reversal event s are staggered so that one shaft is rotating in th e 
forward direction while the other shaft is rotating in the reverse direction. Over time, this sequence of  
events ensures that the processing of the waste mate rial is distributed evenly across the entire cutting 
chamber. 
 
An added benefit is the tendency for wire and similar material, which may have started to wind around the 
cutter shaft, to unwind and dislodge during the shaft rotation reversal process. 
 
The Auto Reverse Programs differ from one another i n the duration and frequency of the shaft rotation 
reversals. Through experimentation, an operator can determine which processing program results in the 
best overall throughput for the type of waste material being processed.
